info.p: fox:wrap on an absolutely positioned fo:block-container: the lines of the page it lands on wrap around it. A4, 72pt margins (the column 451pt wide, its top at 72pt), 16pt lines; each container is written as a word processor's anchored object is, a fixed container in a zero-height wrapper at the head of its anchor paragraph, 150 x 100pt at page y 136, four lines down. 1: at the right margin: the first four lines full width, the seven lines from 64 to 176 (the first legal break after which a line lies below the foot at 164) 301pt wide, the rest full. 2: in the middle of the column (room 150 to 300) with the lines on the left only: 150pt wide. 3: at the left margin, largest side: the lines 301pt wide and shifted 150pt. 4: top-and-bottom: no line beside it, the lines from 64 set below its foot. 5: as 1 with distances 12 18 24 6: the band is 124 to 254, so the lines from 112 to 256 are beside it, 277pt wide. 6: an absolute container 32pt below the top of its paragraph, the second: the band begins at 48 in the flow, inside the paragraph's first line, so its lines from 32 are beside it. 7: a control without fox:wrap: every line full width. 8: the band begins above the box that holds the container (page y 150, the anchor the seventh paragraph): the page's elements are read again from its start with the band known, so the one-line paragraph before the anchor whose text the band crosses is beside it too. 9: the band covers the top of page 2 (page y 72), the anchor mid-page: page 1 ends where it did, and page 2's lines are beside it from its first. 10: a band that the fourth line crosses by its leading only: Word narrows a line whose text crosses the band's top, not one whose leading does, and at the foot a line whose box, with the leading above the text, crosses it (its readings of 2026-10-15), so the fourth line keeps the full width and the eleventh is beside the container. 11: a band beginning inside a paragraph's second line, where orphans keep the boundary: the edge is made there all the same (Word's probe cases 3 to 6 and 9, 2026-10-15). 12: a container as wide as the column: the lines go below it, as for top-and-bottom (Word's probe case 7). 13: a band covering the top of a page that a forced break starts (corpus 3475's logo page): the edge is the forced break, the block carrying it read again from its start, nothing lost. 14: a column-wide band that would push its own anchor past the page's foot (corpus 8362): the page breaks before the anchor, which lands on the next page below the container. 15: a column-wide band ending 8pt above the page's foot (corpus 13544): the content after the edge starts the next page at its top, the clearance to the foot belonging to the page the edge lies on. 16 to 18: two obstacles on one page (corpus 6603's frames): the lines are narrowed by every obstacle whose band holds them, the foot of one is the start of the rest, and an obstacle's top met while another is on is an event as a foot is. 19: two cases in one page-sequence separated by a forced page break, each with its own picture: the scan of a list's first page stops at a forced break. 20: two top-and-bottom frames anchored at the page's top with a gap between them: the body's lines go in the gap, as Word lays a frame's text (the frame-page-bands probe). 21: a frame above every line of its page, anchored at the page's foot (corpus 5218): no edge is taken and nothing moves. 25 to 27: a paragraph's last line fitted above a band together with the border and padding its block closes with (Word's probes of 2026-10-16, m1's bordered empty paragraph): 25: a one-line paragraph whose line fits above a column-wide band but whose 30pt padding and 1.44pt border do not goes below the band; 26: with the padding 0 the border fits and the line stays above; 27: a two-line paragraph whose second line fits but not with its border: that line alone goes below, the widows notwithstanding.
